name: Rochin v. California
court: Supreme Court of the United States
topic: Fourteenth Amendment due process; forcible stomach pumping to recover swallowed evidence; the shocks the conscience standard
summary: Three Los Angeles County deputies forced their way into a man's bedroom, jumped on him when he swallowed two capsules, and had a doctor pump his stomach against his will to recover them. The Supreme Court reversed his morphine possession conviction, holding that evidence obtained by conduct that shocks the conscience violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Rochin is the origin of the shocks the conscience test that still governs substantive due process claims about executive conduct. It is taught for that history and for the limits the Court later placed on it.
coverage: The full opinion of the Court by Justice Frankfurter, the syllabus, and the concurring opinions of Justice Black and Justice Douglas were read from the Library of Congress U.S. Reports scan at https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep342/usrep342165/usrep342165.pdf. The scan is headed 342 U.S. 165, No. 83, argued October 16, 1951, decided January 2, 1952, which confirms the citation.
Justice Minton took no part in the consideration or decision of the case.

The later treatment of Rochin described in this brief (County of Sacramento v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833 (1998)) was read from the Library of Congress scan of that opinion for the companion brief. Lewis says at footnote 9 that Rochin was decided long before Graham v. Connor and today would be treated under the Fourth Amendment, albeit with the same result.
The California District Court of Appeal opinion (101 Cal. App. 2d 140) was not read. It is described only as the Supreme Court described it.

Course materials teach Rochin as the origin of the substantive due process force test. That is consistent with Lewis, which calls Rochin the case in which the Court formulated and first applied the shocks the conscience test. The brief notes that Rochin itself was a criminal appeal about the admissibility of evidence, not a civil damages case.
facts:
The facts are as the Supreme Court stated them, taken from the testimony of one of the deputies. On the morning of July 1, 1949, three deputy sheriffs of the County of Los Angeles, having "some information" that Rochin was selling narcotics, went to the two story house where he lived with his mother, common law wife, brothers, and sisters. Finding the outside door open, they entered and then forced open the door to Rochin's room on the second floor. They found him sitting partly dressed on the side of the bed, on which his wife was lying. On a night stand beside the bed the deputies saw two capsules. When asked whose they were, Rochin grabbed the capsules and put them in his mouth.

A struggle followed in which the three officers "jumped upon him" and tried to extract the capsules. The force they applied did not work. Rochin was handcuffed and taken to a hospital. At the direction of one of the officers, a doctor forced an emetic solution through a tube into Rochin's stomach against his will. The stomach pumping produced vomiting, and in the vomited matter were two capsules that proved to contain morphine.

Rochin was tried without a jury in California Superior Court for possessing a preparation of morphine. The two capsules were the chief evidence against him and were admitted over his objection, even though the deputy frankly described how they were obtained. He was convicted and sentenced to sixty days in jail.

The District Court of Appeal affirmed despite finding that the officers were guilty of unlawfully breaking and entering, of unlawfully assaulting and battering Rochin in the room, and of unlawfully assaulting, battering, torturing, and falsely imprisoning him at the hospital. One of the three judges concurred only because he felt bound by California Supreme Court decisions, which he said law enforcement officers had looked upon as an encouragement, if not an invitation, to such lawless acts. The California Supreme Court denied a hearing without opinion; two justices dissented, writing that they saw no valid distinction between a confession extracted by physical abuse and evidence wrested from a defendant's body by physical abuse. The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari because of the serious question about the limits the Due Process Clause imposes on state criminal proceedings.
holding:
Reversed. Justice Frankfurter wrote for the Court.

The framework. The administration of criminal justice is predominantly committed to the states, and the Court's function in reviewing a state conviction under the Due Process Clause is a narrow one. But the Court also has its responsibility. Due process imposes a judgment on the whole course of the proceedings to determine whether they offend those canons of decency and fairness which express the notions of justice of English speaking peoples even toward those charged with the most heinous offenses. These standards are not formulated as specifics. Due process is a summarized constitutional guarantee of respect for those personal immunities that are so rooted in the traditions and conscience of our people as to be ranked as fundamental, or implicit in the concept of ordered liberty.

Judges are not at large. The Court spent several pages explaining that the vagueness of due process does not leave judges free to apply their personal notions. The limits come from considerations deeply rooted in reason and in the compelling traditions of the legal profession, and the judgment must rest on a disinterested inquiry, a balanced order of facts exactly and fairly stated, and detached consideration of conflicting claims, duly mindful of continuity and change. Due process is not to be frozen at some fixed stage of time or thought.

Application. "Applying these general considerations to the circumstances of the present case, we are compelled to conclude that the proceedings by which this conviction was obtained do more than offend some fastidious squeamishness or private sentimentalism about combatting crime too energetically. This is conduct that shocks the conscience." Illegally breaking into the privacy of the petitioner, the struggle to open his mouth and remove what was there, and the forcible extraction of his stomach's contents was a course of proceeding bound to offend even hardened sensibilities. "They are methods too close to the rack and the screw to permit of constitutional differentiation."

The coerced confession analogy. Due process has long ceased to be heedless of the means by which otherwise relevant and credible evidence is obtained. The coerced confession cases are applications of a general requirement that states in their prosecutions respect certain decencies of civilized conduct; convictions cannot be brought about by methods that offend a sense of justice. It would be a stultification of the Court's responsibility to hold that the police cannot extract by force what is in a man's mind but can extract what is in his stomach. The distinction between real evidence and verbal evidence ignores the reason coerced confessions are excluded: they are inadmissible even if true, because they offend the community's sense of fair play and decency. To sanction the brutal conduct here would be to afford brutality the cloak of law.

Limits. The Court said it was not calling into question state decisions dealing with essentially different, even if related, problems arising from modern methods and devices for discovering wrongdoers. It acknowledged that hypothetical situations can be conjured up shading imperceptibly from this one, but the Constitution is intended to preserve practical and substantial rights, not to maintain theories. On the facts of this case, the conviction was obtained by methods that offend the Due Process Clause.

The concurrences. Justice Black concurred, saying he would reverse under the Fifth Amendment's self incrimination clause, which he believed applies to the states, and he objected that the majority's shocks the conscience, sense of justice, and decencies of civilized conduct standards were nebulous and accordion like, capable of being used to nullify the Bill of Rights as readily as to protect it. Justice Douglas also concurred on Fifth Amendment grounds. He noted that the evidence would be admissible in the majority of states that had considered the question and said he could not agree that those states' rule violated the decencies of civilized conduct; he would exclude words taken from a person's lips, capsules taken from his stomach, and blood taken from his veins when taken without consent, as a definite and workable rule rather than one turning on the idiosyncrasies of the judges.
notDecided:
Whether the Fifth Amendment privilege against self incrimination applies to the states. The majority decided the case on due process grounds; Justices Black and Douglas would have reached the Fifth Amendment.

Whether the officers' entry into the home or the initial struggle, standing alone, violated the Constitution. The Court condemned the course of proceeding as a whole and reversed because the conviction rested on evidence obtained that way.

Whether other methods of obtaining physical evidence from a suspect's body, such as blood tests, violate due process. The Court expressly put aside state cases involving essentially different, even if related, problems. Later decisions addressed those questions.

Any civil liability. Rochin was a criminal appeal about the admissibility of evidence. It did not involve a damages claim against the officers, and section 1983 excessive force law did not exist in its modern form in 1952.

Whether the Fourth Amendment governed the officers' conduct. The Court decided the case under general due process. In County of Sacramento v. Lewis the Supreme Court later said that Rochin today would be treated under the Fourth Amendment, albeit with the same result.
inPractice:
Rochin is taught for history more than for a working rule. Before Graham v. Connor, courts judged police force under the general due process standard Rochin announced: conduct that shocks the conscience violates the Fourteenth Amendment. Graham later held that force used in an arrest, stop, or other seizure of a free person is analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard, not substantive due process. In County of Sacramento v. Lewis the Supreme Court said Rochin itself would today be a Fourth Amendment case, with the same result.

So why does it still matter to an officer? First, the shocks the conscience standard still governs force claims that fall outside the Fourth Amendment, such as injuries to people who were never seized, and the familial association claims brought by relatives of a person who dies in a police encounter. Lewis built directly on Rochin for that purpose. Second, Rochin is the clearest example of force that no standard will tolerate: breaking into a bedroom, jumping on a man to pry open his mouth, and forcing a tube down his throat to retrieve two capsules. The Court said those methods were too close to the rack and the screw.

Dr. Sowards teaches Rochin as the origin of the substantive due process force test and uses it to anchor the idea that there is conduct so far outside the range of acceptable policing that the law will not weigh it at all. Officers should understand that the Fourth Amendment reasonableness test is the one that governs their arrests and detentions, and that Rochin describes the floor beneath every standard.
trainIt:
Teach Rochin as the beginning of the force standards timeline. Put three cases on the board in order: Rochin (1952, due process, shocks the conscience), Graham v. Connor (1989, Fourth Amendment, objective reasonableness for seizures of free persons), and County of Sacramento v. Lewis (1998, shocks the conscience survives for claims outside the Fourth Amendment, and in a sudden pursuit it requires a purpose to cause harm). Students should be able to say which standard applies to which situation and why Rochin would be a Fourth Amendment case today.

Use the facts to teach proportionality and purpose. The deputies wanted two capsules. Ask students what lawful options existed once Rochin swallowed them and why the choices made were condemned by every California judge who wrote in the case. The discussion should surface that the purpose of force in an arrest is control, not evidence extraction by pain, and that no departmental interest justified what was done.

Teach the Black and Douglas concurrences briefly as a lesson about standards. Both justices agreed the conviction had to fall but worried that shocks the conscience was too vague to guide anyone. That same concern is why Graham replaced it with the Graham factors for seizures. Students should understand that the specificity of the Fourth Amendment test is meant to help them, because it tells them what will be weighed: the severity of the crime, the immediate threat, and resistance or flight.

Do not teach Rochin as a civil liability case or as a case about any particular technique. It was a criminal appeal about evidence. The lesson is the floor: some conduct is unconstitutional under any test.
caution: Read in full from the Library of Congress scan. Rochin is a 1952 criminal case about the admissibility of evidence under the Fourteenth Amendment; it is not a section 1983 case and does not apply the Fourth Amendment. The Supreme Court later held in Graham v. Connor that force used in seizures of free persons is governed by the Fourth Amendment, and said in County of Sacramento v. Lewis that Rochin would be a Fourth Amendment case today. The shocks the conscience language should be taught as the substantive due process standard that still applies outside the Fourth Amendment, not as the test for an ordinary arrest.

applications.title: The floor under every standard
applications.body: The Court held that forcibly pumping a suspect's stomach to recover swallowed evidence, after breaking into his room and jumping on him, was conduct that shocks the conscience and violated due process. Some conduct is unconstitutional under any test.

applications.title: Force is for control, not evidence extraction by pain
applications.body: The Court compared the methods used to the rack and the screw and said the police cannot extract by force what is in a man's stomach any more than what is in his mind. Pain inflicted to obtain evidence has no lawful justification.

applications.title: Where shocks the conscience still lives
applications.body: Graham moved arrest and detention force claims to the Fourth Amendment. The Rochin standard still governs substantive due process claims outside a seizure, including the familial association claims relatives bring after a death. Lewis explains how it applies in a sudden pursuit.

applications.title: Every judge condemned the conduct
applications.body: The California appellate court found the officers guilty of breaking and entering, assault and battery, torture, and false imprisonment, yet affirmed because it felt bound by precedent. The Supreme Court reversed. Conduct a court calls torture will not be rescued by a rule of evidence.

quiz.q: On what constitutional ground did the Supreme Court reverse Rochin's conviction?
options: The Fourth Amendment prohibition on unreasonable searches
The Fifth Amendment privilege against self incrimination
The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, because the evidence was obtained by conduct that shocks the conscience
The Eighth Amendment prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment
quiz.teach: The majority held that the methods used offended due process. Justices Black and Douglas would have relied on the Fifth Amendment, but that was not the ground of decision.

quiz.q: According to the Supreme Court's later decision in County of Sacramento v. Lewis, how would Rochin be analyzed today?
options: Under the Fourth Amendment, with the same result
It would come out the other way
quiz.teach: Lewis said Rochin was decided long before Graham v. Connor and today would be treated under the Fourth Amendment, albeit with the same result. Graham governs force used in seizures of free persons.

quiz.q: What was Rochin v. California procedurally?
options: A section 1983 damages suit against the deputies
A criminal appeal challenging the admission of evidence at a state trial
A civil suit against Los Angeles County for failure to train
A habeas corpus petition about sentencing
quiz.teach: Rochin was convicted of morphine possession on the strength of the capsules recovered by stomach pumping. The Supreme Court reversed the conviction. The case did not involve civil liability for the officers.
